quote: In not one single passage of the Old Testament will you find anyone talking about a transcendent wonder at the complexity of the universe.
content: This is a real error, and it is the kind worth conceding cleanly: Psalm 8, Psalm 19, Psalm 104 and the voice from the whirlwind in Job 38–41 are a sustained register of wonder at the created order, and the sentence as written is false. What survives is the essay’s actual argument, which is that these texts also make many checkable claims about history and nature and were understood as doing so. The Wisdom literature’s wonder is not offered in place of factual assertion; Job’s speeches assert a cosmology, with storehouses of snow and foundations of the earth, that its author took to be how things are.

The biology does not support the defense. Cecotrophy is not rumination: the soft caecal pellets are taken directly and swallowed whole, without mastication and without regurgitation from a fore-stomach, which is what the Hebrew ma‘aleh gerah, "brings up what is chewed," describes (Hirakawa 2001, "Coprophagy in leporids," Mammal Review 31). Lagomorphs do move the jaw more or less continuously, which is where the impression comes from and which is why the example is a good one: a Bronze Age observer generalized from a surface resemblance and got the anatomy wrong. That is the essay’s point about the text’s epistemic standing, and it stands.

quote: The orthogonality of religion and factual questions is a recent and strictly Western concept.
content: The allegorists cited did not hold anything like non-overlapping magisteria. Augustine insisted that scripture yield to demonstrated natural knowledge and also insisted that the resurrection, the creation of the soul and the miracles were literal historical fact; Maimonides argued the world’s eternity was undemonstrated and therefore that scripture ruled on it. Their principle is that scripture must be read in light of what is proved, which presupposes that scripture is making claims in the same domain and can lose there — the opposite of a separate magisterium. The doctrine that religion makes no factual claims at all, so that no evidence could bear on it, is the recent construction the essay names.

The essay is not asserting the secularization thesis; it is describing a rhetorical retreat within educated religious apologetics, and it says in the passage the annotation quotes that the majority of religious people on Earth do not accept the separate-magisteria view. That is not a self-contradiction, it is the distinction between what apologists say when pressed and what believers hold. Berger’s recantation concerned the prediction that modernization would erode religiosity worldwide; it did not concern the observation that where the argument is conducted in public, religions have progressively vacated the empirical claims they once defended, which is the trend the essay documents with the retreat from Genesis, from geocentrism and from a young Earth.
